title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Problem III, which converts the alternating 'factorial-type' series s = 1/α − 1/(αβ) + 1/(αβγ) − … into a continued fraction, and then applies the result to e.

(1) Tail recursion. Define the tails t, u, v, … (begun on the previous page). Then s = (1−t)/α, t = (1−u)/β, u = (1−v)/γ, and so on. So
 1/s = α + α/(−1 + 1/t),
 1/t = β + β/(−1 + 1/u),
 1/u = γ + γ/(−1 + 1/v), etc.
Substituting each later expression into the earlier one gives
 1/s = α + α/(β−1 + β/(γ−1 + γ/(δ−1 + …))).
This is Theorem VI, §40. It is a special case of Euler's general series-to-continued-fraction correspondence: the partial sums of the series equal the successive convergents.

(2) Application to e (§41). Start from 1/e = Σ(−1)^n/n!. This gives (e−1)/e = 1/1 − 1/(1·2) + 1/(1·2·3) − …. So α = 1, β = 2, γ = 3, … and
 e/(e−1) = 1 + 1/(1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …))).

(3) Lemma and second example (§42). Subtracting 1 from the result above gives 1/(1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …))) = 1/(e−1).
Euler states as easy (no proof given) the lemma: if s = a/(a + b/(b + c/(c + …))), then a + a/(b + b/(c + c/(d + …))) = s/(1−s).
Proof by unwinding: write B = b/(b+C) and C = c/(c+D). Then s/(1−s) = a/B = a + aC/b. The remaining claim, C/b = 1/(b + b/(c + …)), has the same shape one level deeper, so formal induction closes it.
With s = 1/(e−1) and a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, … this yields
 1/(e−2) = 1 + 1/(2 + 2/(3 + 3/(4 + …))).

Numerical check: truncating deep, the right side ≈ 1.3922 = 1/(e−2). Also correct: e/(e−1) ≈ 1.58198 from the continued fraction.

Purpose: the paper (E593) systematically turns classes of series into continued fractions, building toward Theorem VII and the √2 example on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors. The lemma of §42 is asserted without proof ('haud difficulter demonstrari queat'); it holds formally by the inductive equivalence argument, and in Euler's application convergence is unproblematic.

deep.surprise_reason: Everything here is Euler's well-known continued-fraction correspondence and its classical application to e. These are standard results attributed to Euler and reproduced in standard continued-fraction literature. Nothing appears unfinished or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: 'orinda' should read 'oriunda' ('fractio continua hinc oriunda est').

The stray '$\frac{e}{e-1}$' at the end of the first block is the catchword at the page foot. It is not a separate formula; the full equation e/(e−1) = 1 + 1/(1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …))) follows on the right half.
Print uses 'vnde' and 'obtine-bitur' with long-s typography; the transcription normalizes these. This is harmless.
